Mr. Speaker, at five o'clock I was referring to some of the concerns which I and members on both sides of the House feel about the revisions to this act and how they affect the livestock business. The livestock industry is very important to a large part of Canada particularly to western Canada where the beef cow herd is largely located. If my memory serves me correctly, roughly 80 per cent of the beef cows in Canada are located in the prairie provinces, thus it is a very important part of the economy of western Canada. Section 178 of the act is very important to those involved in the livestock business and to farmers in general.
If we refer back a couple of years, the figures show that roughly 45 per cent of the grain grown in western Canada was fed to livestock there, another 45 per cent was exported and the remaining 10 per cent was used for seed and industrial purposes. Livestock is important to the people involved in its production and sale but it is also important to producers of grain crops. About one third of the production on the prairies is fed to livestock within 30 miles of where it is grown. That gives an idea how important livestock industry is to western Canada.
We are all concerned about stability in agriculture, Mr. Speaker. The problems with roller-coaster prices of recent years are well known. There have been times when it has been difficult to find world markets for our products. When you consider that almost as much of our grain is fed to livestock as is exported, it is easy to realize how important livestock is to a stable base for the western economy. Without a livestock industry, in times of high production and low prices, it would be more difficult to find a market for the grain crops.
A large part of the packing industry in western Canada has been lost in the last ten or 12 years because of variations in


livestock numbers. At the present time there are only three points in western Canada where hogs are slaughtered. There are several points in Edmonton where hogs are still slaughtered. In Saskatchewan, where 1 was born, raised and educated, there is only one point and only one plant that is still in the business of slaughtering hogs, and that is Intercontinental Packers in Saskatoon. Winnipeg is the only point in Manitoba where hogs are still slaughtered. The declining packing industry in western Canada makes it important to be careful about the kind of security offered to the livestock industry in section 178 which is to replace the old section 88 of the Bank Act.
I should like to refer to a couple of things said in recent times by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, how attitudes and how statements can change as circumstances change. Prior to the Quebec referendum, the Minister of Agriculture addressed the Quebec Farmers' Association at Sawyerville, Quebec, on May 7. In part he said as follows:
The 'Crowsnest Rate' and the Feed Freight Assistance Program have reduced the cost of grain shipped into Quebec and thus lowered the cost of producing hogs and poultry here. These subsidies have resulted in benefits for western grain growers, but they have also decreased the natural comparative advantage for livestock production on the prairies and given assistance to livestock producers in the east.
Also, the 'Crowsnest Rate' has favoured the growth in Quebec of processing plants for meat, flour and vegetable oils since products processed in the west are not eligible for the preferential statutory rate, while the raw products are.
That is an interesting statement by a minister trying to get a point of view across just before the Quebec referendum, Mr. Speaker. After the referendum, in a speech to the Canadian Feed Industry Association in Quebec City, the minister had this to say:
On this subject of feed freight assistance, you know it is sometimes said that the program has encouraged eastern pork production to the disadvantage of the west. So I was interested in a study that Dr. Perreault has done which shows that the assistance only amounted to about 50 cents a hog in Quebec on the majority of pork produced here. So the assistance is not much of a factor, especially when you consider how extensive the Quebec feed industry was in the first place.
I find this a rather inconsistent position for a minister of agriculture who should be speaking on behalf of all the livestock producers in the country. In some ways it is unfortunate that a minister who has as his constituency the total agricultural community should find it convenient to make conflicting statements at different times and in different places about the things that concern some of us in regard to this bill.
I think we all agree that changes to section 88 of the Bank Act are needed. Perhaps it is necessary to have some understanding of the way in which livestock is marketed in this country to see the necessity for such change. Livestock is still marketed largely on trust in this country. I think it is fair to say that those of us engaged in this business can do a lot of our selling by telephone when dealing with packer buyers and order buyers who have had past experience with producers. This only works if everyone involved has complete confidence in the system, of course. The old section 88 really did not accomplish as much as it could have in the way of giving producers confidence in the marketing system as it limited their ability to claim against a packing house to roughly
Bank Act
$7500. Anyone familiar with the cattle business knows the expenses that face producers. Fertilizer costs, machinery costs, repair costs, land costs and taxes have all increased substantially since the present Bank Act has been in place. It is a very expensive proposition to raise livestock for sale. A lot of producers sell their stock at a particular time of the year, so it is important that the buyer has the means to pay, otherwise the whole year's work is in jeopardy. Things are different in the case of other farm products. For instance, the dairy industry, because of its very nature, markets on a daily basis. The grain industry can store the product until the market is right and so a whole year's work need not necessarily be marketed at one time. In contrast, a farmer who raises calves may sell them all in one day. We therefore have good reason to be concerned about the old section 88 of the Bank Act. I am aware of several cases of packing houses experiencing financial problems in the last ten or 12 years which resulted in producers being unable to collect what was due to them.
I am familiar with the arguments advanced by the banks and the packing companies to the effect that if the banks are not allowed to take security on livestock, as was the case under the provisions of the old section 88, the packing industry would suffer. These arguments usually refer to the small packing plants. It seems to me the case is exactly the reverse. As we well know, in this country the packing industry is dominated by the "Big Three"-Canada Packers, Burns and Swift, who account for over 50 per cent of the kill. I think those institutions are financially secure, although such an assumption does not necessarily follow when one remembers what has happened in the past year to such large manufacturing institutions as Chrysler and Massey-Ferguson. However, the three large packing houses are public companies and I think it would be quite difficult for them to have financial problems without a great many people being aware of the fact.
Some of the small packing plants are independently operated, family-owned businesses, and are well run. But it is a competitive field and it is not uncommon for companies to get into financial difficulty. If there is any suspicion that one of the smaller packing houses is having financial problems, I think the producers would be hesitant to deal with it. We must do all we can to assure that, irrespective of the size of the packing company or processor, the producer is protected by this act. This would go a long way to assuring that the smaller packer had as much chance to compete with the larger packer as possible. Our concern is that the bill before us does not go far enough in terms of assuring the producer there will be no financial problems and that his product will have prior claim in any bankruptcy settlement until it is paid for. If there is any hint of that not being the case, and I argue strongly that the smaller packer will be disadvantaged as opposed to the major three packers in this country, Swift, Canada Packers and Burns, that simply does not wash as an argument for the banks to use.
It is precisely the opposite. If they were interested in seeing a competitive packing industry, they would ensure as much


Bank Act
financial security in the hands of the producer when dealing with processors as possible. This would go a long way toward seeing that some of our smaller packers have as good a chance to bid on livestock as the larger packers.
If we look at the experience across the line, we see that the Americans have also had some problems. Some of us are aware of the larger problems they had. In 1976 they passed a packers and stockyards act. I will quote part of that act I referred to in the speech I made on second reading of this bill on May 6, as reported at page 772 of Hansard. It is a concern I am dealing with tonight. I quote from the act:
-in effect, that all livestock purchased by a packer, and all inventories of or receivables or proceeds from meat sales, shall be held by a packer in trust for the benefit of all unpaid cash sellers until full payment has been received.
Since that act was put in place in 1976, I understand there has not been one case where a producer has not been fully paid for his product after a financial problem had arisen with the processor or packer. Therefore, to say that nothing can be done is not accurate. We need only look to our neighbours to the south. They put in place legislation which protects producers from some of the problems we are pointing out this evening.
The banks like to have as much security as possible. They like to say that putting in this kind of provision which would guarantee producers full payment, would put an extra burden on the banking industry and cause them added costs in the form of bonding and extra security and, therefore, make them less competitive and less able to do the job. That is nothing but rubbish. It is not borne out in the example we saw across the line in 1976 when the Americans put in their packers and stockyards act. In fact, we have seen the exact opposite. We have seen the packing plants there survive, grow and flourish. Their return to the producer, based on a percentage of the consumer's dollar coming back to the farmers, is greater than the percentage of consumer dollars going back to the producers in this country. So that is another argument that just does not wash. We were Concerned about this when we were in government and the Bank Act was in front of us prior to the last election. There was concern on both sides of the House. When we were in government, I was part of the finance committee which looked at this. One thing that came out during the election campaign was a statement by the Liberal national campaign headquarters. It was part of their election policy.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Their propaganda.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
That is probably more accurate, based on what we see in front of us in the bill and what was promised during the campaign. I will read a section of the Liberal party agricultural platform which was released on January 30, 1980. I quote:
A change in the revision to the Bank Act (section 88) will be made in order to permit better financial security for the farmer, on agricultural produce in transit storage or processing, by providing protection to producers of all agricultural products (not just crop and dairy products) and that protection will be extended to a maximum of $250,000.
That was said during the election. It is interesting to note that the chairman of that campaign committee is our present
Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). One would think that if anyone had been aware of what the policy was and how it was developed, it would be our finance minister. As the finance minister in the new government, one would think he would have seen fit to honour a commitment made to the farmers of this country during the last election.
What happened is that we have a formula. It is based on the most recent annual average index number of farm prices for agricultural products for Canada, published by Statistics Canada, at the time the receiving order or claim is made. That figure is to be multiplied by S400. My understanding is that will roughly raise the limit from $7,500 to $100,000. I certainly agree that is a step in the right direction. However, the principle of this is not attacked. It should not be lawful in this country to let any processor or packer take as security a product from a farmer, or anybody for that matter, and give it to a bank as security without the producer being fully compensated. In the case of financial problems, the processor or packer can give that product to the bank as security, without the farmer fully being paid for it.
Something is not yours until it is fully settled and fully paid for. It goes a little beyond that when you understand the marketing system in this country. As I stated before, it is largely based on trust. Producers deal with agents, order buyers and packing buyers with packing houses on a year to year basis. They do not get a chance to deal with them regularly and keep up to date with some of the problems that may be encountered in the processing plant. Dealing is based largely on trust. A lot of producers could find themselves in the position of not being aware of problems they are getting into, particularly when they feel that their cattle are theirs until they are fully paid for. According to this act, the procedure that is sold to a packing plant can be taken by a bank. The bank would then have prior claim on it over the $100,000 limit. The producer could be out any amount over $100,000. That sounds like a lot of money, $100,000. In fact, it is a lot of money. But if you look at what is involved in raising livestock and getting it to market, a lot of expense is incurred along the way in terms of producing costs. In many cases the farmer is not dealing with his own money. He is dealing with borrowed money, lines of credit, credit accounts with fertilizer dealers, fuel dealers, machinery dealers and repairs. In a lot of cases, he could be out an additional cost over and above his cost of production. Therefore, if we cannot deal with processors and packers with complete trust and confidence, no matter what happens after our livestock leaves our premises, we are calling into question some of the premises upon which our marketing system has been based throughout the years.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), a long-time and well-respected spokesman for the cattle industry in this country in various fora has pointed out very aptly and accurately that on page 188 of the bill subsection (6)(b), "claims of a grower or producer of products of agriculture for money owing by a manufacturer to the grower or producer for such products"-I will not refer to the full paragraph-is incomplete and that there is probably a technical omission


there in the sense that after "claims of a grower or producer" we should insert three words "or his agent" so that the section would read, "claims of a grower or producer or his agent of products of agriculture for money". I think hon. members would agree that that is a technical omission. It would simply mean that a person involved in the marketing of livestock could then use an agent, and the agent would be an extension of the producer himself. In that sense the producer would be covered under the subsection of this act to which I just referred.
Unless we insert those three words within the subsection, it seems to me there is a fairly substantial loophole, if we understand the way cattle are marketed in this country, because many people market cattle through an agent; they do not market them directly. They market them through an agent, and the agent then becomes an extension of the producer himself. If we leave out those three words in the case of a financial problem with the processor, it seems to me we leave open the possibility that the producer would not be protected at all under this act. As I said, when we understand the way the marketing system in this country works, I think it becomes clear that a good portion of cattle and livestock which is marketed in this country is marketed either through or by an agent acting on behalf of a producer. While it may be a technical error, and a minor one, in terms of its significance and its relevance and the act's ability to do the job it was intended to do, I think it would be very useful to have those three words inserted so that the act would read; "claims of a grower or producer or his agent of products of agriculture for money owing" and so forth.
I think that is something we should look at very closely with an eye to putting those words in if at all possible because without them, as I said, I think there is a possible large loophole in terms of what the effectiveness of this act could be.
From my recollection of the finance committee in the previous Thirty-first Parliament, there was much agreement in the committee that the principle which I have tried to outline here should be in the act so that not only the producer but also the people acting on behalf of the producer-in this case the agent of the producer-should be considered an extension of the producer himself. I do not really think there would be many problems about getting an agreement to insert those three words into the act. As I said, this would certainly tighten up the act and make it serve the purpose better than the present act without the addition of those three words.
That about covers the points I wanted to make in relation to this act. I will summarize them briefly. First, this act really does not go far enough. I think the $100,000 is an improvement. I would much sooner have seen the $250,000 which was promised during the election campaign, but 1 think the best option we could have would be to adopt in principle a statement saying there should be no limitation whatsoever on livestock producers so that when they do sell their cattle, no matter what the amount is, they are entitled to full payment of that amount before their produce becomes part of a bankruptcy settlement.
Bank Act
I welcome the change in the definition whereby direct products of the soil and dairy products are now classified in the same way as livestock, which was previously not the case. I pointed out that precisely the opposite should have been the case, since people who market on a regular basis are less susceptible to severe financial hardship. If there is a problem with marketing what they produce on a daily or weekly basis, people in the livestock business market on an annual basis, and we would certainly like to see this act tightened up so that there are no loopholes in terms of agents acting on behalf of producers in the marketing process as we now know it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss if I did not take a little time this evening to make a few comments with respect to the bill which everyone is so anxious to pass here tonight. We have only been at it for five years. The act expired in 1977, and we began the debate relating to changes in the Bank Act two years prior to that. As we all know, the act was extended until now, and we are finally getting around to putting it straight and doing what we should have done in 1977 to make the changes which have been discussed.
There is a lot of mystery about the Bank Act. The average Canadian really does not understand how the banks in this country function. Frankly, I do not understand very much about it either.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: They are waiting with great anticipation. When I said bankers got me into politics, I said so because I started quite a number of small businesses. All of them, incidentally, were successful. None of them went bankrupt.

speechtext: Yet.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
No, they are still going. Because I wanted to have a clean shirt when 1 came to Parliament, I divested myself of most of my business interests. However, I developed a skill in talking to bankers and convincing them of the viability of small businesses which employed usually two, three, five, ten or 120 people. It requires quite a bit of skill today-and did 20 years ago or 25 years ago when I started my first business-to convince a banker that you have something going for you, that you have a better mousetrap, that you deserve a place in the marketplace and that you need some credit to get started.
Our banks do not give venture capital to small businesses. 1 am not making any excuse for this absolute statement. There is just no way that our banks are in any way interested in helping young people to get started in business. Whether that business is farming or in the manufacturing sector does not matter. I do not care if you are a member of the New Democratic Party or any other party; if you cannot walk into your bank manager's office and prove to him beyond all doubt that you really do not need money, you simply will not get any credit.
I always say that in our country there is no single entity, whether it is government or anything else, which has more influence in the marketplace than the banks but which at the same time has less understanding of what goes on in the marketplace, particularly with respect to the small business sector.
The reason I wanted to say a few words about that tonight is that over the last 25 years of frustration and starting businesses-which probably could have been four, five, six or ten times their size if bankers had co-operated-I always said there would be a day when I would get even with some of the bankers with whom I have had to deal.
We do not want to be too unkind tonight, but certainly they do not deserve any credit whatever. The 13 chartered banks in this country do not deserve any credit at all for helping small business. In fact, I would say they deserve the lion's share of the blame for the economic situation in which we find ourselves today because they ignore completely the incredible role which the small business sector plays in our society. It is the small businessman who creates the permanent jobs quickly with the right incentives and in the right business climate. It is the small businessman who always comes up with new ideas. To me, sir, there is not much difference between the bureaucrats who sit around in offices in the nation's capital, public or corporate bureaucrats, and the bureaucrats employed by large corporations. They are nine to five people, they go home on weekends, they take a month's holiday annually and they
cannot care less. It is the small businessman who is out there competing in the manner in which Adam Smith intended, in the free enterprise manner. It is the small businessman who invents the mousetrap and who thinks for 24 hours a day so as to stay ahead of the next guy.
I say that the banks have no comprehension of what is going on in the marketplace and of the role which the small businessman plays. And why should they? Imagine an official of the Chrysler Corporation coming to a bank manager and telling him he needs $100 million. Imagine how much time the bank manager would have to spend talking to small businesses to lend them $100 million! With Chrysler he can do it in a two-hour session and a working luncheon. But here is $100 million and, my God, the branch can lend that sum of money because it is great business. It is not necessary to ask the client for security and tangible assets in the case of a large corporation such as Chrysler because the government is the security. If something happens, the bank can go to the government because the impact on the economy would be so great that the government would have no choice but to bail out the corporation. We have seen recent examples of that.
But let us consider the person who works for that large corporation-and I will get in my dig at the NDP at this juncture. Members of that party come to the House every day and every time one of them is up during the question period he talks about economic nationalism and about all these horrendous things that the multinational corporations do to our country. Yet when one of these multinational corporations comes to us for help, as has been the case of Chrysler-they stand in their place and they scream, holler, assert themselves and demand from the minister that he act right away to save jobs. The reason they do this is the invisible handshake-we have heard of the invisible hand of Adam Smith-between large corporations and multinational unions. They all get together in the board room behind closed doors. They say "there is one multinational corporation which we will have to protect but every other corporation that is not unionized or does not contribute to the NDP coffers can go down the drain." The small businessman is left in the dark and so is the employee of small businesses. I dare say that a person who works for Massey-Ferguson or Chrysler and then finds himself out of a job is no better off or worse off than a person who works at the corner grocery store, the baker, the shoemaker, the plumber or an employee of another small business. He is just as hard up as the other fellow, but the government never comes to the aid of the small business which goes broke. The bank moves in, calls its note and saves its skin. Usually there are enough assets to ensure that the bank does not suffer. I do not know of any bank with which I have dealt, particularly in the north and in the small communities in Canada, which has ever made a bad loan to a small businessman, the reason being that they hardly make any loans to them and when they do, they are protected well enough.
What we have been trying to do in these five years of talking about the Bank Act is, because of our belief in free enterprise and competition, to build in a little more competition. We have


made comparisons with our system here, which is still a mystery. It became a mystery when we first brought in the fractured reserve system according to which the bank lends you a certain amount of money and then is allowed to lend a certain amount of "blue sky", in other words they lend you more money than they have in deposit. However, I do not want to go into the technicalities because that would be too difficult for some of the members of the NDP to understand. What we wanted to do was to build in some competition to match what was going on in the marketplace throughout the country. We have 13 chartered banks in this country. In the United States there are 1,300 chartered banks, all of them competing with each other. If there is a personality conflict between you and your banker, if he does not like your type of proposal or if you cannot convince him of the potential success of the prototype or of the plant where your particular mousetrap would be manufactured, you just go to another bank and sell your idea to them. Eventually you convince someone of the possible success of your idea and you get the money. Indeed, there were several occasions in my business career, one which I remember in particular, which have made me say to this day that the banks become involved in politics. There was a time when the 13 chartered banks in this country simply did not make any loans to small lumber companies because they did not like the government in power. So if you were in British Columbia at that time and you wanted to expand your business, as we did then, you had to go to the United States and get your money there. Lo and behold, there was all kinds of money available because we had all kinds of assets. As for our banks, it did not matter how much you had in assets, how much you had in inventory, how much protection there was under section 88. They said that lumber and wood converting industries did not have a very bright future under that particular government, so they would not make any loans to them. 1 do not know whether this had anything to do with the fact that there are certain people in the larger companies integrated with the multinational companies, who sit on the boards ofdirectorsofthe banks, but certainly there is room for all kinds of suspicion. If you really want to get started in a small new business, you have to go to a foreign country to promote your idea. That is a very sorry state of affairs.
The government is well aware that our banks are not interested in small business, not interested in venture capital. From time to time we have found it necessary to intervene as a government, knowing how important small business is as a sector of the economy, to put in place some measures, to create some institutions which will help the small business sector. An example of that is the Farm Credit Corporation. Why should we need a Farm Credit Corporation in this country? If banks did the business which they were set up to do, that is to make loans to businessmen-and, after all, a farmer is a businessman-what reason would there be for the government to be in the business of lending money to farmers? The reason, as 1 have stated, is that banks are in no way interested in helping out anyone who wants to start a business, regardless of the security they offer. We must remember the farmer who has
Bank Act
worked many years clearing his land and developing a farming enterprise. He has worked for many years and has never made any money. His only reward would be if he sold the enterprise, the farm and the land to his son. Then he could retire and live his declining years in comfort and security. The Farm Credit Corporation started out with good intentions, but it is in no way more equipped to respond to those particular needs. Officials of the corporation will say, "If you want to buy the farm from your father, he should underwrite the loan or perhaps make you a loan". A lot of Canadians are fed up with living in the breeding grounds of human misery in the concrete jungles of our large cities. They want to go out to the country to start farming enterprises. It would probably take at least $250,000 to build a viable farming operation today. At least it would take $250,000 to buy the land and clear it or to buy an established farm. We all know they would not get very much for less than $250,000.
But there are still some people out there who are-should I say-almost crazy enough to think that farm life is worth fighting for. So, they start working in sawmills or on construction. They take their earnings and put them in their farms; they clear a little more land. When they reach the point at which their farms are almost viable, they go to the Farm Credit Corporation to borrow a little money to get them over the hump, to buy that first piece of machinery. They realize it is no use going to the banks. I have established that fact. But, the Farm Credit Corporation says, "If you have not made the major part of your income on the farm, you are not entitled to a loan". Incidentally, they are not entitled to loans if they are in any way involved in provincial or federal politics. They cannot obtain loans from the federal government because there would be a conflict of interest.
The Farm Credit Corporation was established over the years to keep banks honest. Another example is the Federal Business Development Bank, a perfect example of how the government, from time to time, intervenes and hopes to help small businessmen or people in regions where banks are not as well represented as they are in larger centres. As we all know, the Federal Business Development Bank likes to be known as the bank of last resort. Indeed it is, because its interest rates are usually 2 per cent or 3 per cent higher. The government wants to be very careful not to enter into competition with the chartered banks. After all, the chartered banks have a monopoly and they do not want anybody to meddle with that, including the federal and provincial governments. So, the person interested in obtaining a loan must bring to the manager of the Federal Business Development Bank a letter indicating that the chartered bank will not lend him any money. Without that letter he cannot obtain a loan from the Federal Business Development Bank. The bank manager is not required to say why he will not lend him the money, but of course we know why. Then the FBDB will take a look at the person. It will charge an interest rate which is 2.5 per cent to 3 per cent higher. It will take a chance on him and will be lenient if he gets behind in his payments.


Bank Act
The FBDB takes other factors into account, but it is twice as onerous to be tied up with that bank than to a bank of foreign origin. Not only does the Federal Business Development Bank want a personal guarantee, it requires the personal guarantees, of one's wife, one's mother and one's mother-in-law, if it is able to get them. If one has a house and a boat, it wants the title to those. It will make sure, beyond all doubt, that when a person has his head half way out of the water, he has absolutely no security left in order to run to another bank to cash in on some of those assets. Anyone who deals with the Federal Business Development Bank will have no other assets with which to negotiate other loans.
From time to time the government goes to the chartered banks and indicates that it has a particular problem and wants to stimulate the small business sector. It asks the banks to make loans to the small business sector and, of course, there is the infamous Small Businesses Loans Act. They go to the chartered banks and say, "If you make a loan to a small businessman, we will guarantee it. In return we want you to give him a concession on interest of 1 per cent, 1.5 per cent or 2 per cent."
On many occasions I have received telephone calls from small businessmen. For example, one will phone and say, "There is a real demand for the product I am producing. I am in the tourist industry and a new road has been opened. I should be building a coffee shop, a service station, a service centre. I need some money. Where do I go?" Of course I will say, "The banks are set up to give you a small businessman's loan. There is a little concession on interest in return for a federal guarantee". Usually the businessman will call back and say, "I have gone to see my bank manager, but he has never heard of it". I am always very amused by that and then my amusement turns to anger. I will phone the vice-president of the bank and say, for example, "You have a bank manager in Watson Lake who has not heard of the Small Businesses Loans Act. Once you have told him about that act, will you tell him to call me so that I can discuss a certain client with him?" Promptly I receive a call from the manager of that small branch who will say, "I have talked with this client. His credit is good enough that we can make him a conventional loan. He is not entitled to a small businessman's loan". He is entitled to a conventional loan at an interest rate which, of course, is 1 per cent or 2 per cent higher than the government guaranteed loan. So, the poor businessman is tied to the rafters and the bank sticks it to him every time.
Perhaps I should bring my remarks to a conclusion because getting back to what I said at the outset, if I get wound up about banks I become very incensed and carried away. Of course not all bankers are alike. I have dealt with a lot of managers in small branches over the last 25 years who felt the same way as I do. When one requests a $20,000 or a $100,000 revolving loan, the bank manager is required to phone his regional vice-president or manager. For example, the areas in which I started my businesses were usually 700 or 800 miles away from Vancouver. Then the regional manager is required to pick up the phone and call Toronto for an okay. I have experienced that on several occasions. By the time he gets
around to saying, "We will be willing to help you", the opportunity has passed. Usually one has generated enough income in the business by waiting, working 24 hours a day and keeping one's suppliers on the string, that by the time the bank gets around to helping, one does not need the help any longer and can tell the bank to find someone like Chrysler or Massey-Ferguson to give the money to. The banks always say, "We will be willing to help you", and I always say, "Who do you think is helping whom here? I am paying interest and I am creating a job for you". In fact the other day I told a banker that I paid him $7,000 in interest last year. Who is helping whom? I do not want their help. 1 do not need handouts.
I should say something positive about the act because we on this side are supporting some aspects of it. We tried to build into it some competitive features. We tried to give the credit unions a little more room to manoeuvre and to compete on a more equitable basis with the banks. The credit unions and caisses populaires should be entitled to participate under the Bank Act. That was not achieved. In my opinion the act will do little to encourage new charters which would start more banks. I would like to see more banks in western Canada, banks which are sensitive and interested in making loans in mid-Canada and the northern parts of our country. In so doing they would be sharing the potential and development of the north and of mid-Canada. What we have done is a small step in this direction. It is in no way sufficient to suit my particular need. I do hope that after this act is passed we will not wait another seven or eight years before we discuss further changes, which in my opinion are required to the Bank Act. I would prefer to see the committee continue its work. I would like us to continue talking to Canadians so that all of us here in the House of Commons will know just how the banks have been failing our economy and how they have been failing Canadians. This would enable us to see how little they have contributed to the welfare of all our citizens because of their monopoly position.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are on the third reading of the Bank Act and as I understand it the third reading is to discuss the broad general principles of the bill. There is no possibility of changing anything in it on third reading.
I suppose that is the best we could expect from a government which is contradictory in many of its policies. I read today that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) was elated because he was able to get 100,000 barrels of oil from Saudi Arabia at $30 a barrel. I cannot understand that elation when he is not prepared to pay Canadians $20 a barrel, which would keep the money in Canada. It is so contradictory the man in the street is becoming very frustrated.
With regard to the money which is required to operate the industries in the energy field, we are making it almost impossible for those people to get credit. The government professes to be a free enterprise government yet it is holding nationalization over the heads of those in the industry. To a great extent


the smaller industries are dependent upon the multinationals which can get capital. Yet today we see the smaller industries leaving the country. Consequently, this postpones the day when we will have self-sufficiency in energy. At the same time the Prime Minister is chasing around the world trying to get oil elsewhere at double the price at which he can get it right here in Canada. I wonder why he does not enable the smaller companies to continue to receive credit and to operate within Canada by entering into an agreement at a proper price with the producing provinces instead of going half way around the world at public expense and being elated when he can arrange oil at $30 a barrel, probably $38 to $40 by the time the contract is completed. People upon whom we must depend to attain self-sufficiency are finding it very difficult to get credit. There are difficult times ahead. The longer the government waits to pay a proper price for the oil in Canada the longer we will be paying through the nose for foreign oil. It is affecting the credit of this country, which the banks will reflect in their thinking and in their loaning of moneys. As a result there will be hundreds of Ontario, Quebec and maritime boys, now earning good wages in Alberta and Saskatchewan, who will be left jobless in the next few months if this thing is not changed.
We talk about the Bank Act as though it were something that did not affect the lives of everyday people. The Bank Act is an instrument by which we can have good times or we can have poor times. I believe that banks have been responsible for much of the inflation in this country. They say inflation is caused by having too many dollars chasing too few goods. Every time the banks attack this problem they do so by raising the interest rates. They will reduce the number of dollars. And what does that mean? It simply means that no one can borrow the money.
The small businessman the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) detailed here so excellently a few moments ago is left high and dry. He is not able to expand his business. As a result there is less production and people are unemployed. If anyone is able to borrow it is only the wealthy, and the wealthy do not borrow when the interest rates are high. They wait until the interest rates are low before they borrow. That is one reason why they are wealthy. This leaves us with less production. Once again there are more dollars chasing fewer goods and so the interest rates go up again. I wonder how many years it will take the banking system of this country and the Bank of Canada to realize that this is not reducing inflation in Canada. It is just not working. Why do they not work from the other end by increasing production? If you have a pile of money this high and a pile of goods this high you will surely have inflation. The money will continue to rise. But if you have the goods coming up it is a far better way to fight inflation than raising interest rates, which defeats the very purpose. The small businessman cannot produce as much. Sometimes he goes out of business. I know a businessman in this country who is sweating his heart out because the interest rate is eating him up. He is wondering what will happen to his wife and children. The interest rate keeps rising and it is killing him.
Bank Act
Changing the Bank Act as we have been changing it will not affect that type of situation at all. The Bank Act has a tremendous influence over the daily lives of our people. In times of prosperity the banks let the credit out and when the banks begin to draw in that credit they can produce a depression in no time flat. As the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River said a few moments ago, the small businessman is being forgotten. This is exemplified in every case he gave, and we can produce hundreds more of them across this country. The small businessman is being forgotten. Today there is fear in the hearts of the small businessmen because they cannot produce more. Interest rates and unemployment are going higher and higher and production is getting lower and lower. This trend will continue until we begin to increase production.
I will be very interested to see the kind of competition the foreign banks have to offer in Canada. There is not much competition among the banks in Canada today. The situation is similar to the competition between CN and CP. These companies have identical rates in most cases simply because they are controlled by a government regulatory body, yet they are considered to be in competition with each other. In reality their prices are increasing simply because they are running two lines of track when they should be operating on one line if there was real competition between these companies, such as, in the trucking industry, there would be better railway facilities.
If foreign banks are required to operate under the same common policy as the chartered banks I doubt that there will be very much competition. In spite of the fact that many hon. members have a view to the contrary, one way to increase competition in the banking field would be to allow provincial governments to become involved. But it is felt that they might provide too much competition, so the provinces must compete in a backhanded way through such institutions as treasury branches and so on. If it were not for the credit unions, caisses populaires, trust companies and similar institutions, this country would be in a sorry plight.
Too many of the policies of the banks are contradictory. For example, what one pays today on exchange for $100 of American money will be different from what one pays tomorrow. The profits of banks are too high. I recently attempted to exchange some money in Edmonton, and I was horrified at the rate of exchange. The whole situation is a one-way street for the banks. They must pull up their socks and increase their services to the consumers.
I agree with the comments of the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River on the Prairie Farm Credit Corporation. These government organizations are usually formed as institutions of last resort. As a result people are forced to be dishonest in order to get a loan. In fact they encourage you to be dishonest. They tell people to go to their bank manager for a letter saying that the bank will not lend the money. I would not tell a young farmer that he must lie in order to get money from the Prairie Farm Credit Corporation, although many


Bank Act
people are being told to go to the bank manager for such a letter. These corporations lend money at such prohibitive rates that no young farmer can survive. With the high interest rates and the price of land today, the young farmer is sunk before he begins.
These programs are established at public expense as banks of last resort. It would be far better if a bank loaned money on the basis of credit. As the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer) said a few moments ago, this act establishes a maximum amount which livestock dealers may borrow from the banks. Why is there a borrowing ceiling for livestock dealers? There is no ceiling for oil companies, wholesale companies, packing houses or other industries. They may borrow up to any amount. The livestock dealer is just as responsible as any other businessman in the country. I cannot follow this kind of logic, nor can the livestock dealer.
Perhaps the amount of $100,000 will be satisfactory for many farmers, but that is not the point with which I am dealing. There is a borrowing limit for livestock dealers, but no limit for any other group, and this has not been explained satisfactorily to me. We are now on third reading and that clause remains in the bill and will become law within hours. Banks are quite able to deal with loan applications from livestock dealers. They will provide loans commensurate with the collateral, and that is the principle upon which the system should work.
Even with the Prairie Farm Credit Corporation a farmer has two strikes against him. For example, if a farmer buys a combine for $100,000 and the interest is deferred until, say, July, the Prairie Farm Credit Corporation will not loan that farmer the money, simply because he has taken out a temporary interest-free loan. I have received a number of letters of complaint on this very subject. There is a great difference in Alberta between banks, farm corporations and the treasury branches. At one time these institutions were in the same position. But this ridiculous rule came to the attention of the Hon. Marvin Moore, a former minister of agriculture in Alberta. When he learned that farmers were being denied credit because a farm implement dealer gave them a few months of interest-free payments, he changed the regulations. Today, the agricultural corporation in Alberta no longer withholds a loan for this reason. The Federal Farm Credit Corporation has come up with umpteen dozen reasons in this regard, all of which, in my view, are ridiculous.
Such policies do nothing but drive up the cost of food. What they are saying to the implement company is, "Do not give out these temporary interest-free loans and we will give out the money". This has the effect of driving up the cost of production. If these policies continue, it will not be long before the public outcry will become so loud that this clause will be changed and the provinces will be allowed to form banks to compete with the chartered banks.
Such a policy would have the same effect as when the government of Alberta created an insurance company to compete with the private insurance companies. The insurance rates of the government company were lower and in order to compete the other insurance companies had to lower their rates. It is an indication that these insurance companies were charging what the market would bear with no relation to risk, costs or profit. The banks are following this policy today.
There is one other point I would like to deal with, Mr. Speaker, and that is the expansion of credit. Governments have given the banks this tremendous instrument for making money. They have given the banks the sole right to expand credit. Unless people go into this matter very deeply they may not realize what it means. Today the banks extend credit by simply lending, say, $100,000 and then when it is paid back, they mark it off. Then there is the interest on that created money during that period based on how much money a chartered bank has deposited with the Bank of Canada.
As 1 have said in this House before, and will repeat as long as I remain, some of that expansion of credit belongs to the people. It would be a good thing if the banks would even go part way and offer half of the net profit on expanded credit, to build schools and hospitals, for instance. But the banks do not do that; they still make huge profits from the expansion of credit, a privilege given them by the government of the day.
I am not against banks, Mr. Speaker, and I do not mind that they make a profit, but that profit should be reasonable and the banks serve the people. In my view the expansion of credit has gone too far. The people of this country should derive some benefit from it. That is not possible as the act stands but I suppose it is the best we can expect from a government that is so full of contradictions in the energy field. It is pleased to pay $30 or $38 per barrel for foreign oil yet refuses to pay more than $16 or $17 for oil produced in this country. How long will the people accept that kind of thing, Mr. Speaker? Maybe after all the rigs have left the west and the hundreds of Ontario and Quebec workers return without jobs, the Prime Minister will begin to realize what has happened to the country. The government then may realize why people in the west feel alienated, distressed and frustrated. Much of that frustration could be alleviated if the government were to pay a reasonable price for western oil. If it made the same offer as that made by the Clark government, more rigs would come back into the country, more jobs would be created and the whole economy would benefit.
I suppose this bill is the best we can expect at this time, Mr. Speaker. I hope it will be used as an instrument to create more buoyancy in the country.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I should like to refer to some comments made in this House this evening. The amendments offered by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) and already voted upon were dealt with very quietly yesterday by both the Conservatives and Liberals. This evening the hon. member from Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) has spoken about the problems of the small businessman, of the housing industry, of the farmers and of the economy as a whole, yet not one member of


the Conservative or Liberal party spoke in support of our amendments.
Just the other day the minister said that the government did not want to interfere with the banks in a social way, Mr. Speaker. What are we trying to do here? Are we trying to make room for the foreign banks to become competitors in this market? Are we considering the credit unions which, due to the curtailments imposed upon them, cannot compete in the same market as the banks? This bill provides all kinds of privileges for the banks but does not give any relief to the credit unions to allow them to become actively involved in this market.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) brought us the philosophy of the Social Credit party. Mr. Speaker, I have seen some of the philosophy of Social Credit governments in British Columbia. They decided to flood thousands of acres of heritage land, not to provide electricity for Canadians but in order to provide a backup resource of water for the United States. Future generations of Canadians will be denied the pleasure of that bottom land, Mr. Speaker. We have had other projects of that nature under Social Credit governments so I know something of the philosophy expounded by the hon. member for Bow River.
I should like now to deal with the structure of the boards of directors of banks and some of the decisions they make. We run into serious problems when we allow these boards of directors to control the flow of money and direct how it should be invested. The ramifications of this could be very serious indeed.
The Conservative and Liberal members who spoke did not mention the large donations made by banks to their parties. The banks make large donations to both parties, so let us align them, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Where did you hear that?

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
I not only heard it, it is a matter of fact, because it is disclosed in accordance with the law. These are some of the things we should be very concerned about, Mr. Speaker.
Just yesterday the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) asked where I was when the committee was sitting. As he well knows, Mr. Speaker, we are only allowed a certain number of members on that committee and the amendments which we voted on today were the result of their efforts to get changes made to the Bank Act. I am proud of them, Mr. Speaker.
If the other two parties in this House had allowed the amendments to pass, a lot of small businessmen would have benefited, there would be more housing starts in the future and the economy of the country would improve. It is unfortunate that they did not agree with our view, because there was a tremendous opportunity here, after waiting five or six years, to improve the Bank Act. To be honest, the people of Canada have missed an excellent opportunity to have an instrument to serve our needs. I am hearing this throughout my constituency and from other areas of the country. Every day I hear of
Bank Act
concerns about interest rates, housing starts and with regard to various other areas. We know through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation that the need is there because they have conducted studies. In some areas there is a zero per cent vacancy rate, yet we hear about MURB housing, housing for doctors and real estate agents. They can put their money into deferments, apartment blocks and fancy housing which does not meet the everyday needs of the people of Canada.
When considering the Bank Act, we should look at meeting the needs in order to build a future of which we can be proud. We should develop an industrial strategy, conscious that if we invest in one area, we might hurt another section of the country or another business. We must include controls in the Bank Act to ensure that we are protected.
One member stated that even provincial governments are affected by decisions regarding the Bank Act. If they like a government, they feel the banks should not be involved in investments because they might make a government look a little better. Isn't that something, especially coming from a member of the Conservative party. Those are the kinds of concerns we have been expressing year after year. They are very real concerns which affect everyone. Maybe that is what the Liberals and Conservatives want. Maybe they want that kind of society. We in the New Democratic Party have a new vision. If the banks are making that kind of profit, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) should be able to direct them to put their profits into such areas as interest rates so that housing, farming and small business can be assisted and that part of our economy can start moving again.
I also heard the comment that we in the NDP would fight to ensure that Chrysler is a viable business so that the employees would be protected. Naturally we will fight for that. We are not necessarily saying we should give that company money or issue a grant. We say that if money is made available or guaranteed by the government, we should have some equity. If the company later becomes profitable, the government should be reimbursed. If it does not become profitable, we should help make the decisions about what takes place in the company and the people who work for it.
I had the opportunity of visiting Windsor during very trying times. I say that if those kinds of decisions are not made, the government will feel the effects. It will not be Chrysler, but the people of Windsor, the governments involved and the country as a whole will be affected. If that company does not carry on its programs and does not follow through, the social aspects that will take place and the ramifications in the community will affect the whole country.
These are serious matters and we take them very seriously. I resent it when other members suggest that we in this party favour handouts. That is not our philosophy. Our philosophy is to join together in hard times and make an agreement with the companies involved. This proved very satisfactory in British Columbia. One of the Liberals mentioned yesterday many of the programs in which we were involved during our time in


Bank Act
government. He referred to Ocean Falls and various companies in which we were involved. Many of them are now going down under another government. They are being sold off and are disintegrating. We will be back and we will again bring in those kinds of programs. These are concerns of the New Democratic Party. They are the issues we would like to see debated. We offered a tremendous number of amendments to this legislation. They were rejected by the other parties. Therefore, we have no alternative but to decline to support this Bank Act. It is unfortunate that some of the amendments could not have been accepted, but that is something the Liberals and Conservatives will have to live with.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to speak on third reading on the general and broad principles of this very important bill. The banking system in Canada is a stable and acceptable system, althouth not overly responsive in certain areas. It is the primary motive force in our society. It is the real essence of industrial and commercial catalyzation and the growth of our industrial society.
The banking system in Canada has enormous power. It controls to a large degree the recirculation of wealth, the creation of credit, in many instances the very growth of the social structure and social organization in which we live and, to a large degree, the growth and health of the industrial structure of our nation. In connection with the growth of any regional area, the chartered banks play an enormous role. That really diminishes with distance. The influence of a chartered bank in an area reduces in concentric circles around its point of location. As a result, in this nation we have had to grow sub-banking systems such as trust companies, credit unions, treasury branches, the Alberta Home Mortgage Corporation and various types of government institutions.
These have been necessary because of the location of the chartered banks in this nation. Where are the head offices of the chartered banks located in this nation? Let me just say that according to regions the west has three banking institutions with a capitalization of $100 million. The first is in British Columbia and has a capitalization of $25 million.
There is one in Alberta, in Edmonton, which has a capitalization of $40 million. There is one in Manitoba, in Winnipeg, with a capitalization of $35 million. There are three in Ontario, in Toronto, with a capitalization of $275 million. There are four in the province of Quebec, in Montreal, with a capitalization of $425 million. There is one in the maritimes or the Atlantic provinces, in Halifax, with a capitalization of $50 million.
The distribution is such that in the western part of this nation there are three institutions with a capitalization of $100 million. In central Canada there are seven institutions with a capitalization of $700 million, and in Atlantic Canada there is one institution with a capitalization of $50 million.
We all know that the investment effect goes far beyond the extent of capitalization. This nation is a large nation growing in a certain pattern. In western Canada we will be needing more like $200 billion for energy investment in the next ten years plus. To a large degree this capitalization was intended to be generated by the profits of the industry itself. What the federal government has done with its energy policy has been to reduce this self-capitalization and place the industry, again to a large degree, at the mercy of the centralized national banking institutions.
My first point is that if this nation is to grow in accordance with its capability, the government and the national banking institutions must look seriously at their locations in the nation. There is no need to have seven chartered banking institutions headquartered and centralized in Toronto and Montreal. I want to repeat that. There is no need in the future for centralizing seven of the largest banking institutions with a capitalization of $700 million in Toronto and in Montreal.
The government should recognize that there is a need to examine the possibility of relocating the head offices of some of these financial institutions. I can ask a very specific question: Why should not a financial institution-not the largest but a medium-sized one-be located in St. John's, Newfoundland in view of the capacity of the oil industry in that area?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Why not Grand Falls?

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Why should there not be serious consideration by these large banking institutions in terms of examining the head office location in Calgary, where much of the energy industry or the energy capitalization in western Canada is needed? Indeed, why not one in Quebec City? Why should not Quebec City have as its apex centre a banking institution to fan out its influence in concentric circles around that centre? That is what happens with banking institutions. As you go farther and farther from the apex centre of banking, there is less and less knowledge at the banking centre and therefore less and less response. The branch banks do not work very well in that regard, and several people have indicated that we have needed trust companies, treasury branches and credit unions to provide risk and venture capital because risk and venture capital is not provided as you get farther and farther from the centres of these banking institutions. They become too conserv-


ative. They lack knowledge of the outlying points of this nation, which is such a big nation.
It is extremely important that the banking institutions themselves and the government examine seriously the location of some of the chartered banking institutions in this nation. There is a need for change in order to bring balance to this nation from one end to the other. Indeed, western concerns, which are paramount today, could be diminished if there was more control over the formation, recirculation and direction of capital within and from western Canada. One of the reasons for the energy battle which is going on in this nation this very moment is that western Canada is trying very hard to create a capital pool so that that capital can recirculate from its own apexes or points of influence rather than constantly from central Canada.
The second point I wish to make deals again with the power of influence and the power of decision-making with regard to the growth of the national industrial equation which is associated with the chartered banks being located in central Canada. I plead with the financial institutions and chartered banks to look very liberally at a policy of appointing to their boards of directors an appropriate representation from the entire nation rather than just from the centre of the nation.
If these institutions will not move their head offices out, it is very important that they bring into the centre, to the point of decision-making and policy formulation, Canadians who understand fully the aspirations, the desires and the potential of various parts of this nation. It is only then that this nation will experience its full growth potential. It is only then that we will be shifting our population in accordance with capability and ability for development of our vast resources and our vast potential. It is vital that chartered banks and the government be very interested in where the banks get the people to man their boards of directors and that there be a representation from this entire nation on the boards of directors of these chartered banks. There should be a very liberal representation, and I do not mean in a partisan political sense.
1 have just one other point to make, and it has to do with financing exports and imports and particularly Canada's vast potential for exporting not only goods but also technological competence. This nation has educated its population. It has inherent in it a technological competence per capita which is second to none in the world. Indeed, it is even greater than that in the United States.
This technological competence is desired and needed in many places in the world, but technological competence can be exported hand in hand with available capital. I would like to see the chartered banks put together a structure for integrating the use of capital in association with the export of technological competence from Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I believe we can call it ten o'clock, and I beg to adjourn the debate.

CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
1 rise in the adjournment debate with respect to a question I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in his capacity as spokesman in this House for the Canadian Wheat Board. It referred to what was and still is a concern of mine, and a great many producers in western Canada, with respect to compensation to them in light of the American grain embargo, which the Canadian government decided to support. After the invasion of Afghanistan almost a year ago one of the things which was decided upon by the Americans was to impose a grain embargo on the Soviet Union as a method of showing their displeasure with what they were doing in Afghanistan. This country decided to go along with the embargo based on certain concerns. One of the concerns related to how the Americans would conduct themselves in terms of international grain sales. Another, which affects us directly in this country, was the fact that it was agreed by the Clark government at the time that producers of grain should not carry the full expense of Canada's international policies. In this case it was foreign policy. It was decided by the previous government that if it could be demonstrated that there were losses of income to western grain producers they should be compensated by the Government of Canada for those losses. The drop in the price of grain from January to the spring of this calendar year was something in the order of 75 cents a bushel. I think this is documented and can be verified by looking at the grain markets and the grain prices.
The answer I received from the minister back in June was:
This decision was made by the previous government and it is supported by the present government; there is no doubt about that. Obviously, the previous government knew that the decision made last January would have certain effects on volumes and on prices. That is why they put forward the idea of compensation.
It is interesting to note that the Minister of Transport, who speaks in this House for the Canadian Wheat Board, agreed in principle that compensation should be paid. He also said in June in answer to another question in this House that there would be a cabinet paper in a few weeks, at the end of the grain season. Those of us who know something about the grain season understand that the crop year ends on July 31, which has long since passed. The crop year runs from August 1 to July 31. So when the minister referred to the end of the grain season he was referring to July 31. We are now passed the middle of November and are far beyond the end of the crop year with no indication from this government as to what the level will be or, indeed, whether there will be compensation


Adjournment Debate
paid to western producers. During that period we have heard many conflicting statements from different cabinet ministers involved in this matter. We have heard statements by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), by the Minister of Transport and by the minister in the other place who is responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. Last week the Minister of Agriculture said he hoped to have a cabinet decision at the end of November on how much producers will be paid. His colleague, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board disagrees with the agriculture minister and says he does not think a decision will be made until late December, possibly not until January. One cannot help but wonder who is speaking for the government in this connection and exactly what their policy is.
It is unfortunate that we cannot have a clear indication from the government as to what their policy is to be. Just yesterday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan), in reply to a question by a member of the NDP from Saskatchewan, said:
There has never been a complete embargo, only a partial embargo. The way in which it has been phrased is in terms of normal levels of trade in those products. That is still the rule. We are now into a new crop season and we have to try to establish what that means for this year.
So, according to the Secretary of State for External Affairs we do have an embargo. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board says that even though the boycott has been ended, Canada will not increase its exports to the U.S.S.R. to make up for the American shortfall. He said we do not have an embargo but the Secretary of State for External Affairs says we do.
The point is that western producers have lost grain. Our government agreed on the level of exports to the Soviet Union of 3.8 million tonnes, and evidence has been available from independent groups, from universities-the University of Saskatchewan just recently completed a study which said that there had been $67 million in lost sales; there have been other private studies and I have press reports-which say the losses have been in the neighbourhood of $200 million. I think it is very important, before we get too far away from the grain sales we are talking about, that some level of compensation be agreed upon so that the producers in western Canada know whether they can expect compensation from this government. 1 strongly urge that this government make good on its promise to western producers. 1 urge the government to make a statement tonight stating that compensation will be available and indicating the level at which compensation will be provided.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on the U.S.S.R. grain trade restraints and the government's commitment to compensation. I should emphasize that we are talking about restraints on grain trade and not an embargo.
First of all, with respect to our participation at international meetings, a subject which the hon. member question last June,
we have been full and active participants. Granted, the Wheat Board did not go to the Brussels meeting in May, but Canada was represented by the grains' group which consulted fully with the Wheat Board before going. The Wheat Board was represented at the meeting in Adelaide.
There have been several questions recently about the government's position on the restraints. Let me repeat what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) said yesterday. He said that there has been no change in policy. Likewise, the government remains committed to compensation and we expect a determination very soon on the level of compensation.
What often gets lost in this discussion, Mr. Speaker, is that our over-all export performance has been very good. Grain exports were up 20 per cent last year, and the Wheat Board has advised us that they will be able to sell all the grain available for export this year. So the western producer will not suffer.
As far as the price is concerned, things have been looking up since earlier this year when the price was temporarily depressed. Initial payment levels announced in July were up substantially from the preliminary levels announced last March. The continuing trend of strong international prices should also encourage the western farmer and this is something we are monitoring closely to see if any further change is warranted.
All in all, Mr. Speaker, the situation for the western farmer is looking quite positive this year.
