PARKS CANADA-GRIEVANCES OF CORNWALL EMPLOYEES- GOVERNMENT CONSIDERATION THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was gratified to see in Hansard of June 19, 1980, at page 1877, that the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) aspires to "ensuring that the province of Ontario is well served and its interests are looked after." I was gratified that the Deputy Prime Minister should aspire thus, but also I was surprised in view of his budget which is a blueprint for disaster for central Canada. If the Deputy Prime Minister and his colleagues more directly responsible in this area which I am questioning truly acted in the best interests of Ontario, her people and the services that Parks Canada regional office provides, they would have accepted the findings of July 3, 1979, put forward by the ADM for Parks Canada, Mr. A. T. Davidson, and 1 quote his words:
-we should move as soon as possible; that any major regional centre near Toronto would be suitable; but that Peterborough is now the most suitable.
They would have accepted the November, 1979, update from Parks Canada which found, for example, that:
The capital program forecast for the region for the next five years provides for more than 70 per cent of expenditures to take place in locations which would be closer to Peterborough than Cornwall.
They would have acted also upon the conclusion that:
An annual saving of $291,700 is estimated to result from the relocation of the regional office from Cornwall to Peterborough.


Instead they acted upon the needs of a member of the Liberal cabinet rather than the needs of all the people of Ontario. Nonetheless, I am willing to take his word that his is an honest aspiration, sincerely felt if not acted upon. Are his colleagues as sincere? Do they aspire equally to the well-being of Ontario, to the efficiency of government, to the course of action which serves best the majority of Ontario or her citizens and public employees who work on their behalf?
Certainly one could not come to such a conclusion on reviewing the lamentable and drawn-out Parks Canada affair. I am sure members opposite will recall their shameful and quite cynical decision to rescind the thorough and exhaustive eight-year effort to move the Ontario regional Parks Canada office from Cornwall to Peterborough, an effort which was ratified and encouraged by both sides of the House while in government.
The words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on June 9, then, have a sad and ironic ring, coming only a month after the announcement by his colleague, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), that the regional office of Parks Canada should remain in Cornwall.
Or, do I understate the case? Am I being too deferential to the Acting Prime Minister, the Minister of the Environment and their colleagues opposite? Should I not state unequivocally, without a shadow of a doubt, that their decision was an irrefutable demonstration of the worst kind of pork-barrelling, that it demonstrated utterly their political opportunism, that it condemned them forever in the hearts of Ontario citizens and employees of Parks Canada, that it was crass, cynical and manipulative power-mongering of the most disgusting kind? This sits a trifle uneasy with the honourable aspirations of the Acting Prime Minister to ensure the prosperity of Ontario.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Simmons) urged that I borrow a leaf from his book on the matter of parliamentary decorum and recommended that I score "honourable, legitimate political points", as reported in Hansard of May 12. His honourable, legitimate political point was that the Conservative government deferred the move of Parks Canada to Peterborough for ten whole months. I am sure the hon. member will wish to acknowledge that as the Conservative government was in power for only eight months, we could hardly have deferred the decision on that matter for ten.
But the hon. member's claim to honour and legitimacy may be more vulnerable on a further issue. Knowing his concern for right and justice, 1 feel compelled to give him an opportunity to redeem himself. The hon. member went on to remind me that "the announcement to defer" this decision "made on August 3, 1979, was made by none other than the hon. member for Peterborough himself. . . the man who announced the deferral last August". This is an unmitigated falsehood, an untruth, a lie. It is furthermore couched in terms which damn the hon. member to his own condemnation-they are "cheap, cowardly and political".

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-TOXIC CHEMICALS SPILL ON WEST COAST-LEGISLATION TO PREVENT REPETITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question relates to a response I received to a question I put to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). His answer is recorded at page 931 of Hansard for May 12, 1980, and reads in part as follows:
I will examine it and report back as soon as possible.
To date there has been no response or report from the minister. To refresh the memory of the House, it related to the dumping in November of last year of a truck load of dangerous toxic chemicals just south of the Queen Charlotte Islands from a barge en route from Alaska to Washington state. These containers began to appear in the vicinity of Prince Rupert in May. They were and are dangerous to the public. At that time 1 directed my question to the Minister of the Environment. I wish to read a few brief quotations in an attempt to elicit from the parliamentary secretary some response and perhaps a tabling of the report which is due from the Minister of the Environment. 1 quote from a May 9 report:
U.S. Coast Guard spokesman Lieutenant Walters in Anchorage said this morning that he was "89 per cent certain" that a notice to mariners had been issued by the Coast Guard office in Juneau at the time the spill occurred.
Karen Gehing, spokesman for the Aids to Navigation Office in Juneau said, however, that a check of the November records showed that no such notice had ever been issued.
The chemical, which is highly toxic and volatile, is bacteriacide used in oil fields. More than 1.1 parts per million of the chemical over a period of 96 hours is lethal to fish and wildlife. It is also highly corrosive, has a flash point of 83 degrees Farenheit, and is absorbed through the skin.
I wish to quote from a report of May 12, 1980:
The loss, and damage to the ship, was reported to the U.S. Coast Guard in Seattle, but according to Marine Inspection Spokesman Lieutenant Larson, the Coast Guard was not informed of the nature of the cargo. .. U.S. Coast Guard officials in Juneau say they have not yet ascertained whether the drum was a part of the November shipment or debris from some other spill. They say safety precautions prevent the Canadian Coast Guard from getting close enough to the recovered cannister to read identifying marks which might determine its origin.
I trust the parliamentary secretary or the minister will respond to this point since my question relates to whether they are considering or have any intention of bringing in legislation which will allow or require labelling to be properly in place so that these types of incidents will not occur. I quote from the same document:
John Hopps of Marine Inspection in Vancouver said today that while there are recommendations for the carriage of dangerous goods as part of an international shipping agreement, and some regulations are enshrined in federal legislation, they are quite vague in many instances. Even though recommendations do exist for many types of chemicals, it is left to the shipper to enforce these recommendations-
Chris Hatfield, former west coast Emergency Co-ordinator for Environment Canada, said from Vancouver today that regulations for chemical transport are "non-specific and need a lot more work."
Adjournment Debate
"Questions of what to transport, where to transport, and how to transport haven't been looked at yet," Hatfield said ... "It's really a vague area; there are so many agencies, so many chemicals, and no regulations."
My concern, and I trust the parliamentary secretary will address this, is in relation to what comprehensive legislation is concerned. The minister is on record as saying that about 85 per cent of the toxic and hazardous waste in Canada is dumped improperly at the present time. One could hardly go to the public at this point and say that either the corporate sector or the government are adequately handling this situation.
There must be feasibility and financial studies, legislation relating to transportation, storage and handling, regulations and legislation related to trans-boundary movement, classification, technology, treatment facilities, the citing of criteria and public safety and environmental impact. None of those issues has been addressed. It took six months before the Canadian government even knew of this spill. Another six months has gone by without any response from the Minister of the Environment. The concern of the public is very much in limbo at this point.
It is a relevant question to ask how many "Love Canals" are being created at the present moment with hundreds of thousands of tons of carcinogenic and mutagenic material being dumped and, in many instances, the creation of totally new and unknown chemical substances in our environment. Tens of thousands of chemicals are now in use and they are being madly dumped in our environment.
In conclusion, I hope the parliamentary secretary will address both the issue of toxic chemical spills, since 1 have not yet received a report or a response, and as well, the legislative question which I put to the Minister of the Environment on the same day.

On the general issue of jurisdictional concerns within our 200-mile exclusive economic zones and our 12-mile territorial seas, the situation is a bit more complicated than the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), indicates. Fie wrote us on July 28 of this year suggesting that the government should seriously consider implementing or supporting the introduction of east and west coast 200-mile zone legislation parallel to the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act.
The exclusive economic zone concept is a relatively new development in international affairs and is among the items being considered at the ongoing Law of the Sea Conferences.
In January, 1977, Canada proclaimed its 200-mile fishing zones on the east and west coasts. The international community has tacitly agreed to Canada's management of marine life resources in these zones, largely because of the diplomatic negotiations which preceded the proclamation and also because of the assurance we gave that historic fishing rights would be honoured. However, tacit agreement on the management of marine life cannot be considered as a precedent to act
unilaterally to encompass the regulation of shipping in the 200-mile zone. Bilateral or multilateral negotiations should precede any proposed action on our part.
I believe Canada must work within the international framework of the United Nations Law of the Sea and the Intergovernmental Maritime Consultative Organization, 1MCO, to obtain ratification of the various IMCO conventions and their protocols to establish global standards for tanker safety, pollution prevention and the carriage of hazardous and noxious substances. We will not get international support if we act unilaterally, and we probably would suffer setbacks in our trading activity as well. We will achieve our goals much more rapidly if we continue our strong support for the international initiatives.
Ratification of the various IMCO conventions will require changes in Canadian legislation. I assure the hon. member that when such changes are introduced, we will be promoting those which protect or enhance the environment. Meanwhile, this government has been working closely with the United States in harmonizing marine navigation systems and in establishing joint contingency plans.
I want to reiterate my concern and, I am sure, the concern all of us share, about the environmental protection of our valuable marine resources. I can assure the hon. member for Skeena and hon. members generally that Canadian federal officials are working in the closest consultation with their colleagues in the United States to ensure the protection of those resources.
